article_title: Learning: One definition to rule them all?
citation: Martin Lövdén, Isabelle Hansson & Toms Voits. (2026). Learning: One definition to rule them all? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00441-7
title: Umbrella definition of learning as environment-informed information processing that changes system properties and behavioral potential
description: The article proposes a unifying definition: "a system's processing of information from its environment, resulting in a change of system properties that alter its behavioral potential and reactions to this information." It combines structural and functional perspectives: the structural aspect is acknowledged but not specified, while the functional component guides operational definitions. It is intended to apply across disciplines, organisms, machines, and groups, with discipline-specific operationalizations of information and behavior.
requirements: Requires discipline-specific definitions of the terms information and behavior to reach acceptable precision
constraints: Excludes maturation and senescence to the extent these are not based on processing of information from the environment
target_learners: Organisms, artificial systems, groups, and cellular networks, as systems that learn
target_learning_goals: Theorizing and cross-disciplinary communication about what learning is
examples: The article evaluates the definition against desiderata for a good cross-disciplinary concept and contrasts it with prior definitions such as Barron's structured-updating formulation
key_sources: Martin Lövdén, Isabelle Hansson & Toms Voits. (2026). Learning: One definition to rule them all? npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00441-7

article_title: Understanding How Students Use Physical Ideas in Introductory Biology Courses
citation: Watkins, J., Hall, K., Redish, E. F., & Cooke, T. J. (2010). Understanding How Students Use Physical Ideas in Introductory Biology Courses. University of Maryland, College Park. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Reformed University of Maryland Organismal Biology (Org Bio) course
description: An introductory biology course at the University of Maryland reformed to focus on basic principles in biology, chemistry, and physics rather than a "forced march through the phyla." Its organizational framework includes "the relevance of universal physical and chemical laws and importance of diverse structure-function relationships." Pedagogically, instructors made lectures more interactive with clicker questions and class discussions, and dedicated a third of class periods to small group activities including concept-mapping, discussions, and enactments.
requirements: Instructors present equations as referents for biological phenomena and revisit them in discussions of form, function, and evolutionary affordances and constraints.
constraints: The course is a single institutional setting; the authors state their data cannot be generalized beyond this one course.
target_learners: undergraduate life-science majors in introductory organismal biology
target_learning_goals: applying fundamental physical and chemical principles to biological processes
principle-based understanding of organismal diversity, structure, and function
examples: Students devised a model organism with specifications such as small size, fast-moving, underwater, considering physical laws previously discussed to plan how it would function.
key_sources: Watkins, J., Hall, K., Redish, E. F., & Cooke, T. J. (2010). Understanding How Students Use Physical Ideas in Introductory Biology Courses. University of Maryland, College Park. https://www.compadre.org/PER/

article_title: How do particle physicists learn the programming concepts they need?
citation: S Kluth, M G Pia, T Schoerner-Sadenius, P Steinbach. (2015). How do particle physicists learn the programming concepts they need? https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04604
title: UML as a common language for discussing software design, analogized to Feynman diagrams
description: The APC uses the Unified Modelling Language in a lecture combined with paper-and-pencil exercises to establish "a common language for discussing software design issues which goes beyond writing down code or pseudo-code". UML concepts are discussed as analogous to developing formulae or Feynman diagrams to simplify understanding a physics problem, and UML diagrams are then consistently used to present more advanced topics throughout the school.
requirements: Only the UML subset needed to discuss design issues on paper or blackboard is presented, given its detailed formal definition
constraints: The lecture presents only what is needed for pencil-and-paper design discussion, not the full formal definition
target_learning_goals: structured discussion of software architecture and design
examples: UML is used to present class relations and to visualize source code that complies with or refuses the class design principles
key_sources: S Kluth, M G Pia, T Schoerner-Sadenius, P Steinbach. (2015). How do particle physicists learn the programming concepts they need? https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04604

article_title: Sustaining educational and public outreach programs in astronomy
citation: Clarkson, W., Bord, D., Swift, C., Rasmussen, E. J., Matzke, D., Murrell, S., LoPresto, M., Campbell, T., Clubb, R., & Salliotte, D. (2016). Sustaining educational and public outreach programs in astronomy. Whitepaper for AAS Education Task Force. http://www.fordastronomyclub.com/index.html
title: UM-D, HFC and FAAC partnership facilities and programs
description: The whitepaper describes a formalized partnership between a 4-year PUI (UM-D), a 2-year college (HFC), and an amateur astronomy club (FAAC), including "theusebystudentsofeachothers'Astronomicalfacilities,andthedevelopmentof educational materialsusingthem." UM-D operates a campus observatory with an 0.4m telescope and four smaller telescopes and offers an Astronomy minor; HFC operates a 38-seat planetarium used in undergraduate education, K-12 outreach, and free public programs; FAAC has approximately 120 members and runs monthly lecture and public outreach observing events.
requirements: Complementary institutional strengths and formalized partnership agreements between the organizations
constraints: Faculty and staff effort on these initiatives has been nearly entirely voluntary and somewhat ad-hoc
examples: FAAC typically holds 6-7 public planetarium shows per month with the HFC planetarium, one of only two planetaria in the area that do not charge for shows
key_sources: Clarkson, W., Bord, D., Swift, C., Rasmussen, E. J., Matzke, D., Murrell, S., LoPresto, M., Campbell, T., Clubb, R., & Salliotte, D. (2016). Sustaining educational and public outreach programs in astronomy. Whitepaper for AAS Education Task Force. http://www.fordastronomyclub.com/index.html

article_title: We Need to Effectively Integrate Computing Skills Across Discipline Curricula
citation: Murali Mani, Jie Shen, Tejaswi Manchineella, Ira Woodring, Jing Bai, Robert Benard, and E Shirl Donaldson. (2025). We Need to Effectively Integrate Computing Skills Across Discipline Curricula. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00894
title: UM-Flint epidemiology calculators: a GenAI-assisted ounce of computing for health sciences
description: An example ounce of computing developed at UM-Flint, published at a public URL. The authors leveraged developments in software development processes, including GenAI-assisted coding, to create tools requiring only minimal effort for software development, aimed at alleviating math anxiety and low self-efficacy commonly observed in students in epidemiology courses, thereby ensuring increased accessibility of epidemiology concepts.
requirements: GenAI-assisted coding and software development processes to keep development effort minimal
target_learning_goals: accessibility of epidemiology concepts; reduced math anxiety and increased self-efficacy
examples: The tool is available at the URL printed in the article: https://umresearcher.github.io/computingDisciplines/HealthSciences/calculators.html
key_sources: Murali Mani, Jie Shen, Tejaswi Manchineella, Ira Woodring, Jing Bai, Robert Benard, and E Shirl Donaldson. (2025). We Need to Effectively Integrate Computing Skills Across Discipline Curricula. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00894
